sheet-1.description: The map half of sheet 1 of the 1924 Woodbine atlas, drawn at 50 feet to an inch left of a heavy vertical line; the right half of the page carries the title cartouche, a location map of New Jersey, notes on the water works and fire department, a key map of the town at 900 feet to an inch and the street and specials index, which are not part of this map. The drawn area is a strip of the residential grid in the west of the borough along Clay, the only cross street on the sheet, from Adams Avenue at the top to Monroe Avenue at the bottom, with Jefferson and Madison Avenues between. West of Clay only the eastern half of each block is drawn (blocks 148, 158, 168 and 178), and east of Clay the western part of blocks 17, 26, 27 and 30. The sheet is drawn with the avenues running across the page and Clay running down it, so north points to the upper right. Development is sparse: scattered one and two storey frame dwellings, a few outbuildings and stables, and many vacant lots; one dwelling is marked damaged by fire. Water pipes of three and four inches run along the avenues and along Clay, with hydrants at several corners. Street widths of 66 feet are lettered for the avenues and for Clay. Lot numbers are printed along every frontage, and the house numbers are noted in the index as arbitrary. The map shows the regular planned grid of the Baron de Hirsch colony at Woodbine with its long, deep blocks still largely open in 1924.
notes: Clay is Clay Street in OpenStreetMap.
Webster Street, west of the half blocks drawn, is not on this sheet; the left edge of the map is the middle of the blocks.
Placed from the four junctions along Clay only (a two-parameter-free similarity, helmert), since no other cross street is drawn.

Map, 50 ft. Left of the heavy line: half block west of Clay and the block east of it, Adams to Monroe Av (Clay is the only cross street drawn). Right of the line: title cartouche, location map, water and fire notes, key map (900 ft to an inch) and street and specials index, masked out.

sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 of the 1924 Woodbine atlas, at 50 feet to an inch, covers the town centre south of Adams Avenue: Franklin running down the middle of the sheet from Adams Avenue to Monroe Avenue, with Jefferson and Madison Avenues between, the eastern half of the blocks west of Franklin, and the full blocks east of Franklin as far as the west side of De Hirsch Avenue at the right edge. North points to the upper right. The north end along Adams Avenue is the commercial part of the sheet: stores and dwellings, a bakery with ovens, offices, and two buildings marked 'To be moving picture theatre', drawn from plans. Further south the blocks are residential with frame dwellings, stables and sheds. Public buildings include the Woodbine High School and the Woodbine Central School on Madison Avenue east of Franklin, and a Jewish synagogue on Madison Avenue west of Franklin. Water pipes of three to six inches run along the avenues and down De Hirsch Avenue, with hydrants at the corners; widths of 66 feet are lettered on the streets and 250 feet on De Hirsch Avenue, whose railroad corridor lies just beyond the sheet. Below Monroe Avenue a strip of the next blocks is drawn with no exposure noted. The sheet records the business and school centre of the planned Jewish agricultural and industrial colony founded by the Baron de Hirsch Fund.
notes: Franklin is Franklin Street in OpenStreetMap; De Hirsch Avenue is DeHirsch Avenue, today two carriageways either side of the Woodbine Railroad Trail on the former railroad.
The drawn east edge of the blocks at De Hirsch Avenue lies about 25 ft further east than the modern parcel edge of the 250 ft corridor; it was not used as control.
Placed from the four junctions along Franklin only (helmert).

Map, 50 ft. Franklin from Adams to Monroe Av, half block west of Franklin, block east to the west edge of the 250 ft De Hirsch Av corridor (railroad in the middle). Woodbine High School and Central School.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 of the 1924 Woodbine atlas, at 50 feet to an inch, shows the north-west part of the town grid between Webster at the left edge and Clay, and from Lincoln Avenue at the top to Adams Avenue at the bottom, with Jackson and Washington Avenues between; the half blocks east of Clay are drawn to the right edge. North points to the upper right. The area is mainly residential: one and two storey frame dwellings spaced along long deep lots, with stables, sheds and many vacant lots. Along Washington Avenue there is more building, including a garage and a flour and feed store, and a service station near Adams Avenue east of Clay. Community buildings are a Jewish school on the east side of Clay and a synagogue in block 7, both heated by stoves and lit by electricity. Three and four inch water pipes run along the avenues and the streets, with hydrants at most corners. Street widths of 66 feet are lettered, and the sheet's scale bar is drawn in the Washington Avenue roadway west of the middle. Block numbers 103, 118, 128 and 138 and 6, 7 and 16 are printed in the blocks, with lot numbers along every frontage. The sheet shows the planned colony's residential grid west of the business centre, with large areas still unbuilt in 1924.
notes: Webster and Clay are Webster Street and Clay Street in OpenStreetMap.
Map, 50 ft. Webster and Clay from Lincoln to Adams Av.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 of the 1924 Woodbine atlas, at 50 feet to an inch, covers the business centre north of Adams Avenue: Franklin running down the sheet from Lincoln Avenue to Adams Avenue, crossing Jackson and Washington Avenues, with the half blocks east of Clay on the left and the full blocks east of Franklin to the west side of De Hirsch Avenue at the right edge. North points to the upper right. The blocks along Washington Avenue and Adams Avenue are the densest in the town, with stores, dwellings with stores, a garage, a bicycle repair shop, a bottling works with Liberty Hall on the second floor, auto repairing, a bowling alley and a post office. City Hall with the fire department and a bell tower stands at the corner of Adams Avenue and De Hirsch Avenue. The northern blocks toward Lincoln Avenue are residential with frame dwellings, stables and vacant lots. Water pipes of three to six inches run in the avenues and along De Hirsch Avenue, whose width of 250 feet is lettered; the railroad corridor itself lies beyond the sheet edge. Block numbers 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 15 and 16 are printed, with lot numbers on every frontage. The sheet shows the commercial and civic core of the colony town beside its railroad station.
notes: Franklin is Franklin Street and De Hirsch Avenue is DeHirsch Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
The east edges of the blocks at De Hirsch Avenue step by 15 to 25 ft from block to block; they are lot lines, not a straight street line.
Placed from the four junctions along Franklin only (helmert); its block corners at De Hirsch Avenue are carried to sheet 5.
Map, 50 ft. Franklin from Lincoln to Adams Av, half block west of it and the block east to the west edge of De Hirsch Av (250 ft, railroad in the middle); City Hall, post office.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 of the 1924 Woodbine atlas, at 50 feet to an inch, covers the 250 foot wide De Hirsch Avenue corridor and the blocks east of it as far as Longfellow, from Lincoln Avenue at the top to Adams Avenue at the bottom, with Jackson and Washington Avenues between; the edges of the blocks west of the corridor (sheet 4) are repeated at the left. North points to the upper right. Down the middle of the corridor runs the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (Cape May branch, Pennsylvania Railroad) with a siding, a freight depot with platforms and an incline, and the passenger station. East of the corridor the blocks hold dwellings, a coal yard, an auto repair garage and stores; south of Washington Avenue stand the factory of the M.R.D. Hat Co., manufacturers of felt hats, and a vacant factory building near Longfellow. Washington Avenue is drawn 100 feet wide, the other avenues 66 feet. Water pipes of two to six inches run along the avenues and down both sides of De Hirsch Avenue, with hydrants and gate valves. Block numbers 3, 4, 9, 14 and 119 are printed. The sheet records the railroad frontage of the colony town, where its industry and freight handling were concentrated.
notes: Longfellow is Longfellow Street in OpenStreetMap; it now ends at Jackson Avenue, so the Lincoln Avenue junction has no modern counterpart.
The railroad is now the Woodbine Railroad Trail; De Hirsch Avenue is DeHirsch Avenue, two carriageways either side of it.
Control: three junctions on Longfellow (Washington Avenue hand-picked at the drawn centre) and four block corners west of the corridor carried from sheet 4.
Map, 50 ft. De Hirsch Av corridor (250 ft, W.J. and S. R.R. Cape May branch, freight depot and passenger station) and the block east of it to Longfellow, Lincoln to Adams Av; M.R.D. Hat Co.

sheet-6-1.description: The main part of sheet 6 of the 1924 Woodbine atlas, at 50 feet to an inch, lying below a heavy dividing line that separates it from an inset of the Cottage Colony for Feeble Minded Males at the top of the page. It covers the blocks east of Longfellow from Jackson Avenue to Adams Avenue, crossed by Washington Avenue, with Bryant on the right and part of the blocks beyond it. North points to the upper right. The area is on the eastern edge of the built-up town: frame dwellings with stables, wagon sheds, barns and coops on long lots south of Washington Avenue, a concrete block garage near Longfellow, and on the block east of Bryant a public school heated by steam. Only part of the block between Jackson and Washington Avenues is drawn; the rest is marked vacant beyond, and the block east of Bryant north of Washington Avenue (block 11) is open ground. Washington Avenue is lettered 100 feet wide, the other streets 66 feet. Water pipes of three to six inches run along Washington and Adams Avenues and along Longfellow and Bryant, with hydrants at the corners. Block numbers 10, 11, 12 and 13 are printed. The sheet shows where the colony grid thinned out into scattered houses and open lots in 1924.
notes: Longfellow and Bryant are Longfellow Street and Bryant Street in OpenStreetMap.
Jackson Avenue's north side is under the heavy dividing line; its junction with Longfellow, and the Adams Avenue junctions, were hand-picked from the drawn block corners.
Part 2 of the sheet, the Cottage Colony for Feeble Minded Males, about three quarters of a mile south of the town, is drawn above the line and was not placed.

Map, 50 ft, two parts. Part 1: Longfellow to beyond Bryant, Jackson to Adams Av (public school), below the heavy line. Part 2: Cottage Colony for Feeble Minded Males, drawn above the heavy line at another rotation; it lies about 3/4 mile south of the town on the road to Sea Isle City and has no street junction.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Cottage Colony for Feeble Minded Males (about 3/4 mile south of the town, west of the road to Sea Isle City) (no street junction; drawn at its own rotation, only institutional buildings and a water tower; needs hand-picked control on surviving colony buildings (Woodbine Developmental Center) from aerial imagery; not in the reference data).

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7 of the 1924 Woodbine atlas, at 50 feet to an inch, is turned on the page: Bryant runs across the top and Longfellow across the middle, while Adams, Jefferson, Madison and Monroe Avenues run up the page, so north points to the upper left. It covers the blocks south of Adams Avenue between Bryant and Longfellow and the industrial blocks south-west of Longfellow, which reach toward De Hirsch Avenue beyond the bottom edge. The upper blocks are residential, with frame dwellings, stables, cow barns and a feed store. The lower blocks hold the town's main works: the Woodbine Light and Water Co. with its engine and boiler rooms, reservoir and water tower; the Bradstone Rubber Co., with sand blasting and press rooms, served by a railroad siding; the Woodbine Machine Works; the Woodbine Borough Clothing Co. factory, marked vacant; the South Jersey Clothing Co.; a furniture factory not in operation; and a building used for feed storage. Block 169 east of Madison Avenue is open ground. Streets are lettered 66 feet wide, and water pipes of three to six inches with hydrants run along them. The sheet records the industrial quarter of the colony town, where the clothing, rubber and machine works that employed its settlers stood in 1924.
notes: Bryant and Longfellow are Bryant Street and Longfellow Street in OpenStreetMap.
De Hirsch Avenue appears only in the margin note 'To De Hirsch Avenue' along the bottom edge.
'Furne Fact'y' is printed for the furniture factory.

Map, 50 ft, turned on the page (Bryant and Longfellow run across, Adams to Monroe Av up the page). Woodbine Light and Water Co., Bradstone Rubber Co., Woodbine Machine Works, Woodbine Borough Clothing Co., South Jersey Clothing Co.
